title: TwinRead: CONCH + MUSK as two readers, distilled for an offline Arduino UNO Q
tagline: CONCH and MUSK read every tile like two pathologists; at a 10% review budget the fused reader's own uncertainty catches 80% of its errors (CRC), and a 6 MB int8 student is built for an offline Arduino UNO Q (x86 replay today; on-board run pending).
description:
Pathology already uses a second, independent read for hard cases. **TwinRead** treats the two foundation models the organizers highlight, **CONCH** and **MUSK**, as two independent readers of every H&E tile (linear probes on frozen features). It adds a pre-registered fusion rule, a review flag that decides which tiles go to a pathologist, a census of shared blind spots, two custom CUDA kernels, and an int8 student distilled from both readers, built for an offline **Arduino UNO Q** with a USB camera (it runs as an x86 replay today; the on-board run is pending). All numbers are local-subset dev numbers (20k NCT-CRC-HE-100K training tiles, full CRC-VAL-HE-7K test; Camelyon17-WILDS unseen hospital 2).

**What the evidence says.** On CRC the fused reader reaches 0.9555 balanced accuracy vs 0.9480 for MUSK (+0.74 pts; tile-level CI, anti-conservative), but large opposing MUS/STR recall swings cancel and the net gain is mostly tumour recall (+3.6 pts); validation chose the rule by 1-2 tiles, and there is no gain on Camelyon17 or for an open-model control pair (PathGen-CLIP + QuiltNet-B-16). On CRC, at a 10% review budget, the fused reader's own uncertainty catches 80.3% of its errors vs 74.1% for MUSK flagging itself; the learned flag that adds disagreement adds nothing, and on Camelyon17 the twin flag does not beat CONCH alone. The honest conclusion: two readers help by giving a better-calibrated fused reader, not because disagreement is informative per se. The pre-registered val-calibrated threshold over-flags CRC test (25.1% for a 10% target) because validation is near ceiling and val → test is a distribution shift.

**Engineering.** K1 turns raw tiles into both readers' inputs in one CUDA launch, bit-exact to the official transforms (90,131 tiles/s with the input on the GPU in the kernel bench). Inside the CONCH + MUSK embedding run it makes preprocessing ×202 faster than PIL, but only ×1.11 end to end because this batched pipeline is GPU-forward-bound. K2 simulates a USB camera filming a screen (SIMULATION) at 46,315 images/s and makes student-training augmentation ×10.6 faster than torch. The 5.65 M-parameter student ties CONCH in fp32 (0.9415) but the deployed int8 model (0.9219, 6.0 MB) is below every teacher; its value is being offline, small and cheap.

**Status: partial.** Complete: the OPEN and CM local-subset analyses, both kernels (verified, benchmarked, sanitizer-clean), CM and OPEN students and int8 bundles, the device app (run on x86 in replay mode only) and the compile-verified LED sketch (not flashed), the capture rig, the NCSA kit, the host dashboard (127.0.0.1:1777) and figures. Not yet done: UNO Q on-board latency and offline demo (measured when the board is plugged in), real camera captures, and the full-data NCSA Delta runs (kit ready in ncsa/). The CONCH/MUSK-derived student is CC-BY-NC-ND and not distributed; the OPEN bundle is the distributable one. Research prototype, not a diagnostic device.
highlights: Fusion (CONCH + MUSK, local subset): CRC-VAL-HE-7K balanced accuracy 0.9555 vs MUSK 0.9480 and CONCH 0.9413 (+0.74 pts, tile-level CI +0.18 to +1.29, anti-conservative). Large opposing MUS/STR recall swings cancel; the net gain is mostly tumour recall (+3.6 pts). No gain on Camelyon17 (−0.40 pts) or for the open control pair (+0.08 pts).

Review flag at a 10% budget (CRC): the fused reader's own uncertainty catches 80.3% of its errors vs 74.1% for MUSK and 66.0% for CONCH flagging themselves; adding disagreement adds nothing (80.3%), and plain disagreement catches 59.0% (it flags the 5.6% disagreements; the rest of the budget is filled in shuffled order). On Camelyon17 the twin flag does not beat CONCH alone.

Pre-registered before any test label (fusion rule, flag, thresholds), out-of-fold student targets, slide-clustered CIs on Camelyon17; reported as measured, including that the val-calibrated threshold over-flags CRC test (25.1% for a 10% target).

K1 CUDA dual preprocess: bit-exact to the official CONCH and MUSK transforms; 90,131 tiles/s with the input on the GPU (46,157 incl. the host copy). In the CONCH + MUSK embedding run, preprocessing is ×202 faster than PIL but end to end only ×1.11, because the model forward is 89.4% of the time.
K2 camera-of-screen augmentation (SIMULATION): 46,315 images/s, ≤ 1 level per op vs a numpy reference, and ×10.6 faster than torch in student training.

Edge student built for an offline Arduino UNO Q: 5.65 M parameters (1.4% of the teachers' vision towers), 6.0 MB int8; fp32 0.9415 (ties CONCH), 0.9135 at the strongest simulated camera severity; deployed int8 0.9219, below every teacher. On the device the two readers are two heads of one student; the int8 flag agrees with the teacher flag at kappa 0.34. Runs as an x86 replay today; UNO Q latency pending; LED sketch compile-verified, not flashed.
models: wisdomik/QuiltNet-B-16 (reader B, OPEN pair; chosen on validation)
timm mobilenetv4_conv_small (edge student backbone, pretrained trunk)
datasets: 1aurent/NCT-CRC-HE: NCT-CRC-HE-100K 20,007-tile class-balanced subset (17,349 train / 2,658 val, group-disjoint) + full CRC-VAL-HE-7K test (7,180 tiles)
wltjr1007/Camelyon17-WILDS: 7,500-tile subset (train hospitals 0/3/4: 4,500; val hospital 1: 1,500; test hospital 2: 1,500)

images.caption: System overview: CONCH and MUSK read each tile (K1 preprocessing), a fused reader and review signals s1-s4 follow, and a K2-trained int8 student is built for an offline Arduino UNO Q (x86 replay today). The full-data Delta runs and the on-board run have not been done.

Fused vs single readers with 95% CIs. CONCH + MUSK fusion gains +0.74 pts on CRC (tile-level CI, anti-conservative); no gain on Camelyon17 hospital 2 or for the open control pair. Local-subset dev numbers.

Review flag: errors caught vs review budget. The fused reader's uncertainty (s3) does the work; the learned flag with disagreement (s4) adds nothing; the pre-registered threshold over-flags CRC test. Right: reader errors per class, darkest = the 53 confident shared errors. Bottom: 8 of them (real CRC-VAL-HE-7K tiles).

K1 dual preprocess: bit-exact; 90,131 tiles/s with the input on the GPU (46,157 incl. the host copy); ×202 vs PIL inside the embedding run, ×1.11 end to end (forward-bound). K2 camera-of-screen augmentation (SIMULATION) and its effect on student training. RTX 5060, shared GPU.
K2 output on real CRC-VAL tiles at increasing severity: a SIMULATION of a USB camera filming a screen (warp, stain jitter, display gamma, moiré, glare, defocus, noise, JPEG).

Edge student vs teachers on CRC-VAL-HE-7K: fp32 ties CONCH, the deployed int8 model is below every teacher (int8 costs 2.0 pts for CM, 2.7 for OPEN); 1.4% of the teachers' vision-tower parameters. UNO Q latency pending.

Device app on the x86 desktop, not the UNO Q (labelled in the image): REPLAY mode, the distributable OPEN int8 bundle on a real CRC-VAL-HE-7K tile. The bars are two heads of one student network, not independent readers. The latency shown is the x86 host's. Captured with headless Chromium (the Playwright MCP browser was locked).

Host dashboard (127.0.0.1:1777, headless-Chromium screenshot): headline tables read from results/headline.json and the tile viewer with both readers' calls, the fused call and the pre-registered flag (confident shared errors shown).

hardware: Arduino UNO Q (Debian on 4x Cortex-A53, STM32U585 MCU with the 8x13 LED matrix) plus a USB camera on a USB-C hub. Implemented: an offline device app (camera or replay -> crop + tissue check -> int8 student via onnxruntime -> AGREE/REVIEW with reasons) with a local web UI, a Bridge-RPC LED-matrix sketch (compile-verified for arduino:zephyr:unoq, not flashed), SHA256-verified bundles and an offline installer, and a screen-capture rig with parity-checked frame markers (simulated captures: 8,000 trials, 7,572 accepted, 0 wrong labels). Runs today on x86 in replay mode. The demo camera films a screen, not a microscope. Pending: on-board latency and the offline board demo (measured when the board is plugged in), and real captures.
how_to_run:
cd twinread-conch-musk-edge
bash run_demo.sh --smoke   # no GPU/network: headline JSON, figures, manifest tests, dashboard check
bash run_demo.sh           # data -> OPEN embeddings -> analysis -> student -> bundle -> figures -> dashboard http://127.0.0.1:1777
bash run_demo.sh --with-cm # + CONCH/MUSK local subset (needs HF access)
event_scaleup: The NCSA kit in ncsa/ is written and statically tested; it has not been run on Delta. Plan: on the login node install CONCH/MUSK and pre-download weights (compute nodes are offline) and stage NCT-CRC-HE-100K from /projects/bfqi/shared/datasets; J1 (<= 0.5 h A100) checks the environment, JIT-builds K1/K2 for sm_80 (asserted), runs the GPU K1/K2 correctness tests (including offline CONCH/MUSK loads) and a short K1 benchmark; J2 (<= 1.5 h) embeds the full 100k + 7k CRC tiles with CONCH + MUSK through K1 (reference fallback); the same pre-registered analysis runs on a Delta CPU node into results/delta/; J3 (<= 1.5 h) distils the CM student on full data with K2; J4 is spare (second seed or the OPEN pair). Target <= 10 A100-hours of a 30-hour budget; another reader pair is one PAIRS entry.
limitations: Local-subset dev numbers (20k of 100k CRC training tiles; 7.5k Camelyon17 tiles); the full-data Delta runs were not run.
CRC has no slide/patient ids: CRC CIs and McNemar tests are tile-level and anti-conservative; validation is group-disjoint, not guaranteed slide-disjoint.

The CRC fusion gain is fragile: large opposing MUS/STR recall swings cancel and the net gain is mostly tumour recall; the rule was chosen by 1-2 validation tiles; no gain on Camelyon17 or for the open pair.

The review flag's value comes from the fused reader's uncertainty, not disagreement; the pre-registered val-calibrated threshold over-flags CRC test, and on Camelyon17 the twin flag does not beat CONCH alone.
Confident shared errors (0.74% of CRC tiles) cannot be caught by any two-reader disagreement signal.
The deployed int8 student is below every teacher on test; int8 drift is larger on test than on validation.

Nothing has run on the UNO Q yet: the device app has run only as an x86 replay; on-board latency, the offline board demo and the LED sketch on hardware are pending (the sketch is compile-verified, not flashed).

The device's two 'readers' are two heads on one shared student backbone, far less independent than CONCH and MUSK; the deployed CM int8 flag agrees with the teacher flag at kappa 0.34 and recovers 33.3% of teacher-flagged tiles.
All camera numbers are SIMULATION (K2, simulated rig captures); the demo camera films a screen, not a microscope; no real captures yet.
Kernel throughput is measured on a shared GPU (estimate); sm_80/sm_90 builds are compile-checked only.
The CONCH/MUSK-derived student is CC-BY-NC-ND and not distributed; only the OPEN bundle is distributable.
Triage curves and the tile viewer use a post-hoc reproduction of the frozen fits (verified to match review.json exactly); the gallery and viewer need the git-ignored local data.
Research prototype, not a diagnostic device; no clinical validation.

lay.what: TwinRead lets two AI models look at the same small patch of a tissue slide. It works like two doctors giving separate opinions. It combines their answers and marks patches a pathologist should check again. It makes a small copy for a cheap offline computer board. That copy has not run on the board yet.
lay.why: Second opinions catch mistakes, but they cost a second expert's time. If software can point to the uncertain patches, a pathologist can spend review time where it matters. A small offline version could someday help clinics without slide scanners, powerful computers or reliable internet.
lay.impressive: When only one in ten tissue patches is sent to a pathologist, the combined model's own doubt catches 80.3% of its mistakes on a public colon tissue test set of 7,180 patches. The better single model, checking itself the same way, catches 74.1%.
